searchText: Can someone remind me if the frontend will be audited and IPFS hosted? And by audited I mean including all of its dependencies. And the build pipeline (if the build output isn't what is audited). I think it is very important that the UI people uses be IPFS hosted, not centrally hosted, because without that I don't think we will have credibility to future people if they cannot look at the code that most people *actually* ran. At the extreme, one can imagine the web host just sending the toxic waste to a central server and saving it instead of deleting it. If the UI isn't content addressed and fully audited, we cannot verify that didn't happen. <nicoserranop> I can try to deploy the react UI in IPFS but I'm not sure if the wasm code for computation is going to have issues in any way :S <trent_vanepps> > <trent_vanepps> Front end will be audited, not sure how far the dependency review will go tho (re @kzg_ceremony_bot: <Micah> Can someone remind me if the frontend will be audited and IPFS hosted?) Just auditing the frontend is pointless if it isn't content addressable **and** (this is important) most people don't use the content addressed version. If everyone just goes to `https://central-website.ru` and executes "whatever the browser returns", then those people are *effectively* just delegating their participation to whoever controls the `central-website.ru` domain when they went to it. If we have 10,000 people participate in the ceremony but 9900 of them just used `https:/central-website.ru`, then your ceremony only *actually* has 101 participants. Just because the code executes on a user's machine doesn't mean the user is the participant. If I convince my friend to double click an executable on their machine, I can't then claim that my friend participated because they may have been running some malicious code that I sent them. They didn't take any steps to verify/validate that they were running the correct code (like using an existing content addressing system built on a P2P network). In fact, I would even go so far as to argue that it is almost pointless to have a centrally hosted version of the page, because those people aren't actually increasing the chances that some toxic waste is burned, nor are they helping prove to future people that some toxic waste was burned. At best, it is a PR move appealing to those who don't fully understand the point of the process. Is there some reason you think you won't be able to execute WASM from a statically served site? <nicoserranop> > <nicoserranop> So far I have had some problems with http headers and our wasm code. But I'm looking how to set this headers in IPFS (re @kzg_ceremony_bot: <Micah> [reply]: Is there some reason you think you won't be able to execute WASM from a statically served site?) Hmm, why does the WASM care about HTTP headers? I would assume you have some WASM, you fetch it, and you execute it locally. Re: IPFS: If you can statically host/run the page then you can IPFS host it. A good test of this is to drop all of the content into a folder on your computer and then double-click index.html without any server. If the page works like that, it'll almost certainly work via IPFS. <nicoserranop> > <nicoserranop> The problem is that web browsers check that the content is coming from a cross origin isolated source to execute wasm (the files should come with a specific http headers to allow browsers execute the wasm code). In terms of a react app, I think it would work in IPFS seamlessly. I will keep you updated on how this goes 😊 (re @kzg_ceremony_bot: <Micah> Hmm, why does the WASM care about HTTP headers?) Where is the WASM coming from if not from the same origin as the rest of the site? Is it not just a file that is served the same as everything else? <CarlBeek> The implied context is that the "main" contribution site is hosted at `ceremony.etherem.org` <CarlBeek> Micah, the expectation is that there should be a static IPFS deployment. The reason people are not fully committing to this now is we've been having fun getting the WASM (cryptography) blobs to run well in all browsers. People are nervous to commit to this for now as things are regularly breaking & unbreaking and we are not on top of that _yet_... All that said, the goal is absolutely to have a 100% static (IPFS) deployment with all working browsers.
